objectives: Trace how an injury turns membrane fat into arachidonic acid, and arachidonic acid into prostaglandins, thromboxane and leukotrienes.
Tell COX-1's everyday jobs apart from COX-2's job at an injury.
Explain why aspirin's effect on platelets lasts for the rest of each platelet's life.
Predict what ordinary NSAIDs, COX-2 selective NSAIDs, aspirin, glucocorticoids and leukotriene modifiers change, and the price of each.

nsaid.prompt: An ordinary NSAID such as ibuprofen plugs both COX-1 and COX-2 for a while. What happens to pain, swelling and fever, and to the stomach shield?
choices: Pain, swelling and fever fall, and the stomach shield thins
Pain, swelling and fever fall, and the stomach shield is untouched
Only the airway squeeze eases
Pain and swelling rise, and the shield thickens
nsaid.why: Plugging COX-2 lowers the prostaglandins behind pain, swelling and fever. Plugging COX-1 lowers the stomach's prostaglandins too, so the shield thins and platelets clump less.

cox2i.prompt: A COX-2 selective inhibitor plugs COX-2 and leaves COX-1 working. What happens to pain, swelling and fever, and to the stomach shield?
choices: Pain, swelling and fever fall; the stomach shield stays near normal
Both fall
Neither changes
Only platelet clumping falls
cox2i.why: COX-2 makes the prostaglandins at the injury, so those fall. COX-1, which keeps up the stomach shield and platelet clumping, still works, so both stay near normal.

aspirin.prompt: Aspirin sticks a tag onto COX that never comes off, blocking COX-1 almost completely and COX-2 less. Platelets cannot make new COX. What happens to platelet clumping?
choices: It falls, and stays down for the rest of each platelet's life
It falls for a few minutes, then recovers
It rises
It does not change, because aspirin acts only on COX-2
aspirin.why: Platelets have no nucleus, so they cannot build new COX to replace the tagged one. Their thromboxane stays low until new platelets replace them.

steroid.prompt: A glucocorticoid works upstream: it makes cells produce annexin A1, which holds back phospholipase A2, and it stops cells making extra COX-2. What happens to prostaglandins and leukotrienes?
choices: Both fall, because less arachidonic acid is freed for either road
Only prostaglandins fall
Only leukotrienes fall
Both rise
steroid.why: Holding back phospholipase A2 frees less arachidonic acid, the raw material for both roads, so prostaglandins and leukotrienes both fall; less COX-2 cuts the injury's prostaglandins further.

ltm.prompt: A leukotriene modifier such as montelukast blocks leukotrienes where they act on the airways. COX is untouched. What happens?
choices: The airway squeeze and airway swelling ease; pain and fever stay
Pain, swelling and fever fall
The stomach shield thins
Everything falls
ltm.why: The block sits only on the leukotriene road, so the airway squeeze and the airway swelling that leukotrienes drive ease. The COX roads carry on, so pain, fever and the stomach shield are unchanged.

quiz.stem: Which enzyme frees arachidonic acid from the cell membrane?
choices: Phospholipase A2
Cyclooxygenase (COX)
Lipoxygenase
Thromboxane
quiz.why: Phospholipase A2 snips arachidonic acid out of the membrane's phospholipids. COX and lipoxygenase work on it afterwards, and thromboxane is a product, not an enzyme.

quiz.stem: Lipoxygenase turns arachidonic acid into which signals?
choices: Leukotrienes
Prostaglandins
Thromboxane
Histamine
quiz.why: Lipoxygenase makes leukotrienes, which call in white blood cells and squeeze the airways. Prostaglandins and thromboxane come from the COX road; histamine is not made from arachidonic acid at all.

quiz.stem: Which job belongs to COX-1 rather than to COX-2?
choices: Keeping up the stomach shield, every day
Making most of the inflammatory prostaglandins once inflammation has built up
Making leukotrienes
Freeing arachidonic acid from the membrane
quiz.why: COX-1 works all the time: its prostaglandins keep up the stomach shield, and in platelets it makes thromboxane. COX-1 also helps at the very start of an injury, but COX-2, made in quantity over the following hours, becomes the main source of inflammatory prostaglandins.

quiz.stem: Why does a COX-2 selective inhibitor usually upset the stomach less than an ordinary NSAID?
choices: It leaves COX-1, which keeps up the stomach shield, working
It also blocks the stomach's proton pumps
It works only inside the joints
It thickens the stomach's mucus
quiz.why: The stomach shield runs on COX-1's prostaglandins, which a COX-2 selective inhibitor spares. Its price lies elsewhere: less prostacyclin from blood vessel linings raises the risk of heart attack and stroke.

quiz.stem: Aspirin's effect on platelets lasts long after the drug has left the blood. Why?
choices: Platelets have no nucleus, so they cannot make new COX to replace the tagged one
Aspirin is stored inside platelets and released slowly
Aspirin blocks thromboxane's receptor for good
New platelets are made with aspirin already inside them
quiz.why: Aspirin tags COX for good. Most cells simply build fresh COX, but platelets cannot, so their thromboxane stays low until they are replaced by new platelets.

quiz.stem: Someone takes ibuprofen, an NSAID, for a sprained ankle. Which pair of effects fits?
choices: Less pain and swelling, and a thinner stomach shield
Less pain, and stronger platelet clumping
No change in pain, but less asthma
More fever, and a thicker stomach shield
quiz.why: Plugging COX-2 eases pain and swelling, and plugging COX-1 thins the stomach shield and lowers platelet clumping. NSAIDs can make some people's asthma worse, not better.

quiz.stem: Why do glucocorticoids lower both prostaglandins and leukotrienes, while ordinary NSAIDs such as ibuprofen lower prostaglandins and thromboxane but not leukotrienes?
choices: They act upstream, holding back phospholipase A2 through annexin A1, so less raw material reaches either road
They plug COX and lipoxygenase directly
They block leukotriene receptors on the airways
They tag COX for good, as aspirin does
quiz.why: Glucocorticoids make cells produce annexin A1, which holds back phospholipase A2, and they stop cells making extra COX-2. With less arachidonic acid freed, both roads slow. NSAIDs act further down, on COX alone, so leukotrienes carry on.

quiz.stem: A child with asthma takes montelukast, a leukotriene modifier. Which effect fits best?
choices: The airway squeeze eases, while pain and fever are unchanged
Pain and fever fall
The stomach shield thins
Platelets clump less
quiz.why: Montelukast blocks leukotrienes where they act on the airways, so the squeeze eases and attacks are less likely. It leaves the COX road alone, so prostaglandins, pain and fever are untouched.

takeaways: Injury switches on phospholipase A2, which snips arachidonic acid out of the cell membrane: the raw material for prostaglandins, thromboxane and leukotrienes.
COX-1 works all the time: its prostaglandins keep up the stomach shield, and in platelets it makes thromboxane, which makes them clump.
COX-2 is made in quantity at an injury; its prostaglandins widen and loosen vessels, sensitise pain nerves and, in the brain, cause fever.
Lipoxygenase makes leukotrienes, which call in white blood cells and squeeze the airways in asthma.

Ordinary NSAIDs such as ibuprofen plug both COX enzymes: less pain, swelling and fever, but a thinner stomach shield and less platelet clumping. COX-2 selective inhibitors are gentler on the stomach, though not risk-free, and spare platelets, but they raise the risk of heart attack and stroke.
Aspirin tags COX for good; platelets cannot replace it, so its antiplatelet effect lasts for the rest of each platelet's life.

Glucocorticoids act upstream, through annexin A1 on phospholipase A2 and by stopping COX-2 being made, so prostaglandins and leukotrienes both fall. Leukotriene modifiers ease the airways and leave COX alone.
